jawi.summary: A vision-language adapter that reads printed Jawi off a page image and writes it back out in Rumi. Fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL-3B with QLoRA, it cut character error rate from 82.51% to 17.35% on extraction and from 90.59% to 16.48% on transliteration.
jawi.context: Jawi is the Arabic-Malay script used across Malay and Indonesian print, and most readers today cannot parse it. Opening one Jawi page takes two steps in order: pull the Arabic characters off the image, then transliterate them into Rumi under the PEJYD spelling rules. Linguists, historians, and philologists digitising Jawi documents need both steps from one image.
approach: Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct with QLoRA in Unsloth, at 4-bit NF4 quantization and bfloat16 mixed precision.
Generated synthetic Jawi text from several Arabic and Jawi fonts, then mixed it with crops from books, newspapers, and historical documents.
Compared synthetic-only, authentic-only, and combined data in a three-way ablation, then kept the Skenario C checkpoint from epoch 3.
Scored both scripts with CER plus WER on Rumi, then published the adapter with a Gradio demo.
result: Extraction CER fell from 82.51% (zero-shot Qwen baseline) to 17.35%; Rumi transliteration CER went from 90.59% to 16.48%.
Word error rate on the Rumi output fell from 107.08% to 39.36%.
Figures come from the held-out 10% of authentic pages: 790 test images in the thesis write-up.

pacu-pintar.summary: The machine learning half of Pacu Pintar: a Random Forest that sorts a learner's pace into consistent, fast, or reflective, plus a FastAPI service that turns that label into LLM-written study advice. Built with one teammate for the Asah capstone.
pacu-pintar.context: Pacu Pintar is an AI learning-analytics platform for an online course site. Its ML component had to answer two questions about each learner: what pace they study at, and what advice would keep them moving. The repo README names the two needs behind it: learners want motivation and suggestions, and they cannot see their own progress.
approach: Derived pace features from course activity: study duration against scheduled hours, spread of study hours, and completed versus viewed module counts.
Trained a Random Forest to label each learner consistent, fast, or reflective.
Served predictions through separate FastAPI pace and advice endpoints, leaving feature calculation to the backend rather than the API.
Sent the pace label, exam average, and course name to an LLM for the advice text, with a plain template fallback when no API key is set.
result: The pace classifier reports about 90% accuracy across the three classes.
The pace endpoint answers in roughly 50–100 ms on the repo's own measurements.
The capstone closed with the Best Capstone Project award at Asah, January 2026.

memory-vault.kicker: Persistent memory layer for any LLM
memory-vault.summary: A Python layer that gives any LLM memory across sessions: it captures conversation turns, extracts facts, compresses old context, and injects the relevant memories into each new prompt. Published on PyPI as memory-vault, currently 0.1.2.
memory-vault.context: Most assistants start every session with no memory of the one before. Replaying the whole transcript into the next prompt is not a real fix either, because the context window fills up. Memory Vault AI sits between the app and the model so only the facts that matter travel with each request.
approach: Split storage into four memory types — episodic, semantic, working, procedural — so raw turns, extracted facts, session context, and preferences age differently.
Retrieved memories by vector similarity over local embeddings instead of keyword matching, which keeps the system runnable offline.
Compressed old episodic memories into summaries and held the injected block to a 2000-token default budget.
Exposed one core through four modes: Python SDK, REST API, CLI, and an MCP server for Claude Desktop and Cursor.
result: Version 0.1.2 is live on PyPI for Python 3.11 and up, under MIT.
Four memory types, four access modes, and 6 built-in MCP tools.
Local-first by default: ChromaDB plus sentence-transformers embeddings, with SQLite for metadata and no external database.
